title: AI Promised to Organize My Clutter. Here’s the Messy Result
author: Alexis Berger

Companion app’s search function works well. Affordable at $20 per pack.TIREDOnly useful if you update the app whenever you move or add an item. Photo-scanning technology makes some errors. Stickers can leave residue.A key ingredient to feeling organized is having a space that’s organized. That logic also helps explain the ubiquity of the junk drawer. It’s simply not realistic to have a dedicated spot for every item you own, so assigning a single destination where you can house all the leftover stuff makes sense. That is, until you can’t find your utility scissors or flashlight or stamps or favorite highlighter or double-sided tape when you need any of those things.Regular organizing conventions won’t help you keep track of everything in your junk drawer—or any other storage area, for that matter. For example, nicely labeling your boxes is great, but if you lose track of where you put them, you’re toast. Also, that box labeled “kitchen stuff?” You definitely don’t know every item that’s inside. The clever SmartLabels system, which uses a QR code sticker for the outside of a bin, box, drawer, or other location and a companion app to keep a digital inventory of its contents, could help with each of these organizational pitfalls.The system is simple to use, but its value in functioning as an up-to-date digital inventory of your belongings depends heavily on how often you update the app. The app won’t know, for instance, if you absentmindedly stow away your double-sided tape with your wrapping paper instead of putting it back in the junk drawer where it is cataloged. You’ll also need to remember to add new items to the app as you add them to a bin in question. But if you’re a gold-star user of SmartLabels, they do stand to help you keep track of your treasures.Photographic MemoryPhotograph: Alexis BergerEach package of SmartLabels includes 48 unique QR-code stickers (four sheets of 12 codes each). After you download the free SmartLabels app (compatible with iOS and Android), fire it up and select the QR code sticker you want to use for the bin in question. The app will prompt you to take a photo of the QR code, then it’ll ask you to photograph the contents that you’re going to store. Every item must be clearly visible, so you can’t simply dump random products in a box and snap a photo. If the camera can’t see an item, the app won’t be able to catalog it. The app is free, but you can opt for a premium subscription ($15 per year) that offers exportable PDFs and spreadsheets of your SmartLabel inventory, among a few other benefits. Businesses might be interested in this capability, but the average home organizer doesn’t need it.I first tried SmartLabels with my kitchen junk drawer. Full disclosure, the photographing stage of this process led me to do a preliminary cleanout, in the same vein as “pre-cleaning for the house cleaners.” So, without various lids to since-lost reusable water bottles, expired insurance cards, and random old receipts, I was able to arrange the contents in a single layer and snap a photo in the app.Photograph: Alexis BergerThe app then created an AI-powered itemized inventory of what it recognized in the image and assigned an estimated monetary value to each, I presume for business or insurance purposes. The prices it listed were in the right ballpark, though not perfect. It also failed to correctly identify a few products, like mistaking my Gemi hand sanitizer for liquid blush and not knowing that my bag of batteries labeled “OLD” indicates that they’re all expired and I’m collecting them to drop off at a designated facility. Both misses are understandable (the hand sanitizer does look more like a cosmetic than it does Purell) and are easy fixes because the descriptions are editable in the app. The app also failed to catalog highlighters, pens, and a checkbook. It’s easy enough to add those, with or without a photo.It’s super important to take the time to cross-reference your photo with the inventory the app generates before you finish out this step. If something is mislabeled or missing from the list, you won’t be able to search for the item in the app, which renders the system a bit useless. Multiple people can access the labels by sharing an account on their respective phones, though two different accounts can’t access the same label. And you must have the app for the QR code to work at all.ScreenshotScreenshot: Alexis BergerScreenshotScreenshot: Alexis BergerI also used a SmartLabel to create a record of everything in my son’s box of baby keepsakes. I find this to be a great use case for the system, because I’ll rarely need to open the box, take items out, or add in anything new (it’s a sad truth that he’s not a baby anymore!). While lack of use minimizes the risk of losing items, it also fosters forgetfulness, and I’m glad I have photo evidence via SmartLabels that I have my little guy’s “coming home from the hospital” outfit stowed away for safekeeping.You can take a photo of the physical location of the box so you know exactly where in your home to find grandmother’s engagement ring, for instance. Opening the app to see the ring is listed as being in a box on the third shelf of your closet will save you a bunch of time—so long as you don’t move the box around after you take the picture without updating the app accordingly.Do You Need It?Therein lies my main hesitation with SmartLabels: The system is great if you don’t move around your items after you catalog them. In some cases, this is fine, like if you’re moving to a new home and you need to know where everything is located for the short-term task of unpacking. Another solid example is my son’s baby memory box, which I’m not planning to futz around with. For any storage space you’re not accessing often, SmartLabels is a clever and functional solution.For other areas, the system is less applicable because the items are likely to move around or change completely, and the app won’t know unless you manually update it. It’s arguably useful for a junk drawer like mine, because I could see myself having no idea where to find my flashlight in the event of a power outage. While the contents of my junk drawer may change (or more plausibly, grow), as long as I leave that flashlight in there, it’ll still be there when I search for it on my app.Photograph: Alexis BergerThere’s also an aesthetic issue with sticking a QR code on a drawer in my kitchen—the look is hardly Nancy Meyersesque. Do beware that if you put the sticker somewhere you intend to be impermanent, you might want to have some Goo Gone on hand. Knowing I didn’t want the QR code to live on my kitchen drawer forever, I very lightly placed it there for testing purposes. When I removed the sticker, there was a bit of adhesive residue I needed to rub off.The sticker didn’t pull off any paint or leave any damage, but had I put some elbow grease into my initial application, that might not be the case. To that end, the app still works even if you place the QR code sticker somewhere else, or choose to not use it at all. If you search your app for “flashlight” after initially scanning the item into the appropriate entry, the app will still know where it is. If you ditch the sticker, you just won’t be able to scan the QR code as a shortcut to its associated inventory list. For storage boxes or for organizing bins that live in less frequented areas of your home, the stickers aren’t an eyesore.While I could see the SmartLabel system as helpful for tracking important documents in a folder or a fireproof case, keep in mind that SmartLabels use AI technology to analyze the photos you upload. The company claims it uses AI that doesn’t store any data for long-term use or train on your photos. Even so, I’d probably refrain from uploading a photo of your Social Security card.For general home organization and labeling, you’d have to be near-constantly updating the app in order for the system to remain helpful. That may be overkill in favor of general labels for spaces like your pantry, file cabinets, and kids’ play area. But for rarely used items, heirlooms, and events like a move, they’re a solid, affordable solution.Power up with unlimited access to WIRED.
